Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when money moves. So if you bill a customer in June but they pay in July, the sale shows up in June. The same goes for bills: an expense is recorded when you incur it, even if you pay later. Cash-basis accounting does the opposite — you only record income when you receive cash and expenses when you actually pay them.

Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing profitability and matches revenues with the costs to earn them, which helps with planning and comparing periods. Cash basis is simpler and can make short-term cash flow easier to see, so small or very cash-focused businesses sometimes use it. Larger companies and formal financial reporting usually use accrual accounting because it shows business performance more accurately. If you want, I can pull authoritative references (IRS or accounting standards) next.

Accrual accounting records income and expenses when they happen, not when money changes hands. If you send a bill to a customer, you record the sale right away under accrual—even if they pay later. If you get a bill from a supplier, you record the expense when the service or product is received, not when you pay. Cash-basis accounting waits until cash is actually received or paid. Under cash basis you only count income when the payment lands in your bank and count expenses when you pay the bill. Accrual gives a clearer picture of ongoing business activity because it matches money earned with the costs that created it. Cash basis is simpler and can show your immediate cash flow more clearly. Small businesses often start with cash basis because it’s easy, while larger or growing businesses use accrual to plan, compare across time, and meet reporting requirements.

You record expenses when they are incurred (for example, when you get a bill), even if you pay it later. This matches revenue and the costs that created it, so it shows whether the business actually made or lost money over a period.

Which to use: cash is easier and reflects actual cash flow; accrual gives a more accurate picture of ongoing performance, especially if you have invoicing, inventory, or delayed payments.
